questions.question: Comprehension: Read the following passage and answer the questions given after it. Over the past few weeks, several firms have released their financial results for the first quarter (April-June) of the ongoing fiscal year. These results provide some clues on the prevailing economic scenario. Three broad trends emerge. One, FMCG major HUL witnessed an uptick in volume growth in rural areas, perhaps indicative of a pickup in rural demand. Two, IT major Infosys has lowered its revenue guidance for the ongoing financial year to 1-3.5 per cent from 4-7 per cent earlier, pointing towards considerable uncertainty in major global markets. Three, banks seem to be posting healthy numbers, as credit growth remains strong. These are, however, only preliminary trends. A more comprehensive picture will emerge once a larger number of firms in the listed space unveil their results. Sluggish rural demand has been a cause of concern. However, after witnessing double digit declines in the past, with inflation moderating, HUL is seeing an uptick. Alongside, data from FADA also shows that sales of two-wheelers picked up in May and June, after contracting in April. These trends sit uncomfortably with other data points. For instance, the number of households availing work under MGNREGA in the first quarter of the year was higher than in the same period last year, indicating the absence of other more productive forms of employment. Further, a recent RBI report had also pointed towards a moderation in real wages in rural areas. However, HUL’s results also signal a resurgence among smaller players in some categories — in product categories such as tea and detergent bars, small players are seeing much faster growth than larger players. This is a healthy sign considering the concerns over smaller players being squeezed out, and bigger firms cornering a larger share of the market. But, alongside, the commentary accompanying IT firms points towards slowing demand for services in developed markets. For instance, Infosys expects some clients to stop or slow “transformation programmes and discretionary work”. Perhaps reflecting this slowdown, the country’s services exports have already begun to see a moderation. For firms, the operating environment, both external and internal, remains shrouded with uncertainty. Across developed markets, there is ambiguity over the extent of further monetary policy tightening, and the implications for growth. There are expectations that the US Federal Reserve will raise rates when it meets next (its next meeting is scheduled for July 25-26). However, with growth being healthy, expectations of a soft landing are gaining traction. On the domestic front, while the RBI expects the economy to grow at 8 per cent in the first quarter, growth is expected to taper off thereafter to 5.7 per cent in the fourth quarter. Inflation is expected to remain within the central bank’s target range, though the risks from weather related events will require close monitoring. During this period of uncertainty, policy should be guided by the objective of maintaining macroeconomic stability Q34. ONCE notorious for its skewed sex ratio and deep-seated cultural preference for the male child, Haryana has over the years managed a steady improvement in the sex ratio at birth (SRB). The king mandated that day was to be treated as night and vice versa. Everyone complied out of fear of execution. In this topsy-turvy kingdom, everything, regardless of its value, was priced at a single duddu. A guru and his disciple entered this city and were perplexed by its practices. While the guru quickly discerned that they were in a kingdom of fools and advised his disciple to leave, the disciple chose to stay, lured by the cheap prices of goods. He feasted on the inexpensive food and grew considerably large and stout. One day, a thief died when a wall, weakened by age, fell on him during a burglary attempt. His brother sought justice, blaming the owner of the house, who in turn blamed the bricklayer that constructed the weak wall. This led to a comical blame game involving a dancing girl and a goldsmith, with the fault eventually coming full circle back to the original homeowner. The king, in his foolishness, decided to execute someone for the death of the thief. But the rich merchant, deemed the prime culprit, was too thin for the stake they had prepared for the execution. The fattened disciple, now plump and sizable, was deemed a perfect fit. As the disciple awaited his unfair fate, he prayed to his guru who, having mystical powers, arrived in time. The guru cunningly convinced the king that the first person to be executed on the stake would be reincarnated as the next king. Both the guru and disciple feigned a desire to be executed first. Believing them, the king and his minister, hoping to be reborn into their current positions, secretly went to the execution ground and met their demise. The next day, when their bodies were discovered, the city was in turmoil. The guru and disciple, on the verge of leaving the chaotic city, were begged by the people to become their new rulers. They agreed, but only if they could change the nonsensical laws. The kingdom returned to normalcy under their wise leadership, with the day and night resuming their usual roles and sensible economic practices reestablished. Q42.
